prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength made frequency measurements at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part for optical lattice clocks, credited to Katori and Ye. After reading all eight statements, the case looks stronger on the points I care about most. The magic-wavelength condition is a simple, original idea that removes the dominant systematic of a many-atom optical clock by design, and it has been carried to the 10^-18 level and reproduced in several laboratories with Sr, Yb and Hg, with agreeing frequency ratios and fibre-linked comparisons. That is reproducibility in the sense an experimentalist can check, and it is the property that separates this entry from several others on the list. It has also produced new measurements: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, tighter bounds on drifting constants and on dark-matter couplings, and clock-based geodesy. Round 1 sharpened the framing. Johansson, Pearce and Mehlig are right that the citation must rest on the demonstrated lattice-clock concept and its 10^-18 performance, not on a redefinition of the second, which is a decision of a metrology body and not a scientific criterion. I withdraw that point as support for the timing. The case stands on the physics already done.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 prize for the comb and the 2012 prize for ion control remains the strongest objection, and the committee can fairly ask whether this is a new discovery or a very successful refinement of precision timekeeping. I answer that the earlier prizes honoured a way of counting optical cycles and control of single trapped particles, whereas the lattice clock is a different mechanism, a neutral many-atom ensemble in which the perturbation cancels by design. Still, that answer depends on a tightly worded citation, and a sceptical reader may not accept it. Second, I cannot settle priority myself. Katori's 2001-2003 proposal and early strontium work, the JILA accuracy programme, and the roles of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hollberg and Hinkley need to be checked against the primary literature by an outside expert before a final vote. A two-name prize leaves real contributors out and I do not want to pretend otherwise. Third, the measurable impact so far lies mainly in metrology and fundamental tests, and the broader external validation has not yet come.

responses.point: Danielsson holds IceCube (B010) as a single part with Halzen and Karle, argues that attribution difficulty is not a scientific objection, and notes that my own first choice also omits Lemonde, Takamoto and the comb tradition.
responses.response: He is right that attribution trouble is not a physics objection, and I accept the correction: my eighth place for IceCube reflects my limits in judging the astrophysics and the credit inside a large collaboration, not doubt about the diffuse flux, which several channels confirm. He is also right that B043 is not free of omissions. The difference, as I see it, is one of degree and checkability. For the clocks the claims can be written down and tested against dated publications, and one expert review should settle priority between two groups and a small number of others. For IceCube the AMANDA lineage, ice calibration, optical modules and the analysis leaders all enter, and we do not yet agree on whether the third name is Yoshida. I would not stand in the way of B010 if the experts clarify credit and a second telescope such as KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD adds independent confirmation. That is a reason to keep B010 as a strong candidate for a later year, not for this one, and I leave it outside my alternatives only because I rank B006 and B028 higher as measurement-based achievements I can judge.

responses.point: Eriksson asks how I weigh a new state of matter nobody predicted in that form (twisted bilayer graphene, B029) against a metrology advance whose headline consequence, the redefinition of the second, has not happened.
responses.response: It is a fair challenge, and I do not claim that the clocks must outrank the moire discovery. I weigh them on three tests. First, stability of the result: the flat-band prediction and the correlated insulators are reproduced, but the superconductivity depends on sample and twist angle and the pairing mechanism is open, whereas the clock uncertainty budget has stayed stable across laboratories. Second, attribution: the experiment has a first author, Yuan Cao, outside the three names, and the wider moire community has claims, which is a more serious cut than the one the clocks face. Third, timing: I would accept that the redefinition of the second is not a prerequisite, as Johansson and Pearce argue, so I do not use its absence against the clocks and the same logic means I should not use the unsettled pairing mechanism too harshly against B029 alone. On balance the moire case is a strong candidate in a few years, once sample reproducibility and credit are clearer. I would move toward it if an expert report resolved the experimental credit cleanly and the field produced a settled account of what the correlated phases are.

responses.point: Johansson says that a redefinition of the second is a policy decision and not a scientific criterion, and that the citation should name the lattice and the magic-wavelength concept explicitly.
responses.response: I agree on both points and have changed my wording accordingly. My round-1 mention of the redefinition as approaching was context, not support, and the citation I now propose says invention and development of optical lattice clocks, with the magic-wavelength trapping stated, and it leaves out any mention of the second. I would add that Johansson's own judgement matters here: he ranked the clocks sixth in his opening ballot and moved up after reading the arguments, and he first ranked circuit QED. Since he has said he should recuse on B023, I note that my WACQT overlap with him is institutional only, and I would not argue for or against circuit QED on any ground other than the scientific one, where my ranking was fourth, for the credit cut among four names and the timing after the 2025 prize.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from IceCube to the clocks because the credited pair has the least dispute, and he admits he cannot adjudicate priority between Katori and the Ye group.
responses.response: I share his reasoning and also his limit: I can judge systematics and reproducibility, but historical priority is a question for an outside reviewer, and I would ask the chair to request one expert report on the early lattice-clock record, covering the Katori proposal, the first strontium lattice measurements and the independent Lemonde and Hollberg-lineage work. I would also resist reading five of eight members as scientific agreement. The support is real but partly an alignment around the lowest-dispute attribution, as the chair's own summary says, and the committee should decide on the evidence for the clocks, not on the count. If the expert report finds that priority is genuinely split, I would rather widen the list by a name up to the three-person cap than defend a cleaner credit that the record does not support.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps defect-mediated two-dimensional melting (B020) as his first choice, accepts B043 as defensible, and wants the citation to rest on the lattice concept and demonstrated 10^-18 performance.
responses.response: I accept his framing request and the citation now follows it. I also take seriously that his preferred part rests on a clear and tractable mechanism, a property I respect. My difficulty remains the experimental side: the hexatic phase is established firmly only in some colloidal and film systems, and others show first-order melting, so I cannot say what a citation would state as confirmed in nature. If experts could point to a clean experimental statement, for example the colloidal two-step melting as the decisive test, I would reconsider it as a later candidate. For this year the clocks remain ahead because the measurements agree to many digits across laboratories.

responses.point: Lindroth reads the clocks as a discovery about what a quantum system can be made to do, separate from the comb and ion prizes, and keeps Bloch, Greiner and Zoller (B006) only as an alternative because Cirac's claim is equally strong.
responses.response: I agree that the difference from 2005 and 2012 is the many-atom neutral lattice with magic trapping, and that is how I would defend the citation. On B006 I agree that the four-name problem is real: Bloch, Greiner and Zoller is the trio I favoured, but Cirac's theory contribution to the Hubbard-model proposal is of equal standing, and dropping him is not obviously fair. That is why I hold B006 as an alternative and not as a second part. I also do not favour a two-part prize this year: no combination with another achievement fits within three people while keeping the clock pair intact, and a weak second part would dilute a well-supported first one.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees magic-wavelength lattice clocks as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; this depends on the citation wording and I cannot settle it by physics alone.

Priority between Katori's proposal and early demonstrations and the Ye group's accuracy work, and whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow or Hollberg-lineage contributions need a wider credit; an outside expert report is needed and I cannot verify the primary record from the materials here.
Whether the pair should be extended to a third name if the expert review shows split priority.

If the clocks are not chosen, whether B006 or B028 is better supported; each has an attribution problem (four names for B006, and the Borde, Pritchard and Kasevich split for B028) that I have not resolved.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. I am at Lund in atomic physics and know the Svanberg, Hall and laser-spectroscopy tradition, but I have no collaboration with the credited names. For circuit QED (B023) I disclose institutional overlap with Johansson through the WACQT leadership team. For any configuration involving quantum memories or rare-earth-doped crystals I would recuse, and none is on the shortlist. My company interest in Deep Light Vision is unrelated to any shortlisted part.
